column2: Almost every day, Pollock arrives in his beat-up car, wheezing up the driveway, and goes looking for Bill; no one knows whether he is going to hug Bill and weep over his suffering as an artist or pick a fight Words: Elaine: “I always thought Jackson himself might blow up. Anywhere. Anytime.” Atmosphere: Nervous waiting, perpetual fear, a hiccuping car announcing the crisis Stakes: Pollock's compulsion toward Bill, between a need for approval and violence

Chaet, in a fury, reports that Keller called Cézanne the greatest faker in history in front of his students sent to the Met; Albers bursts out laughing, finds it the funniest story he has ever heard, and calms Chaet at once Words: “Don't forget, boy, we've already won this battle... it's a joke” Atmosphere: The young man's anger, the old man's serene laughter Stakes: A cold war between moderns and academics at Yale

Cage announces a class devoted to Williams Mix; the hour comes and no student shows up; they have all understood that it would mean hours of cutting and splicing magnetic tape. Atmosphere: Silent comedy: the master alone with his magnetic tape Stakes: The students choose self-preservation over avant-garde adventure

Cage gives each performer time brackets during which he or she does anything at all; Rauschenberg, precocious and joyful, is said to play Édith Piaf records; one of his White Paintings hangs from the ceiling; Olson's presence remains uncertain, memories are hazy. Atmosphere: Orchestrated chaos, a simultaneous and indeterminate event Stakes: The principle of collage carried into performance: the birth of the happening

Charlip sets a program at the press in 8-point type, so small that it takes a magnifying glass and tweezers; he prints it on cigarette paper and stacks the programs near the entrance with a bowl of tobacco, an ashtray on every seat. Atmosphere: tiny, ephemeral, playful: the program is smoked while one listens Stakes: the ethos of chance enters everyday gestures

For her thirteenth birthday, Hermine receives presents made by Rauschenberg and Rockburne; Rauschenberg arranges thorny branches, blades of grass, petals, sand, and a figurine on sensitized paper, exposes it to light, and removes everything: the shapes remain as white silhouettes on a blue ground. Atmosphere: Intimate, summery, a childhood in the midst of the avant-garde Stakes: The private gesture that condenses the sensory revelations of the summer of 1952

Rauschenberg sets the Tworkov girls huddled in a mass of ferns, then photographs Hermine in profile, body slumped, hair loosely tied, in natural light with a shallow depth of field that flattens the space between the foliage and her. Atmosphere: Pensive, leafy, sharp outlines Stakes: The equality of figure and ground, the very perception the college teaches

In the spring of 1952, Cernovich prints Duncan's poem in red ink on laid paper; Twombly, probably helped by Rauschenberg, makes the linocuts for the cover in the months after Rauschenberg's breakup with Susan Weil. Words: The first lines of the poem printed on the sheet. Atmosphere: Coral-red ink on laid paper, intimate and risky. Stakes: A queer love poem printed in the segregationist South at the height of the Cold War.
A wire sculpture nearly ten feet tall swings like a pendulum as visitors pass, fascinated and baffled. Atmosphere: puzzled fascination Stakes: the work refuses categories: neither sculpture nor craft

Cage is out of town and lends his apartment to Rauschenberg; Rauschenberg works there on his series of Black Paintings; to thank him, he paints a Black Painting over the pink and sand No. 1 that Cage had bought at Betty Parsons in 1951, a work itself painted on a canvas by Sue Weil. Stakes: The work as palimpsest: three layers of authors and affections.

Rauschenberg poses nonchalantly in front of the four-panel White Painting, a camera or a third person's gaze capturing the artist and his work Atmosphere: Deliberate casualness, a dandy's pose Stakes: The artist becomes the subject of his own work

Rauschenberg enlarges and dry-mounts the photographs of Twombly's paintings for his grant application, then reflects that Albers would have approved of such care Words: He says he made large, carefully mounted enlargements, before concluding: “Albers would have liked that” Atmosphere: A craftsman's pride, an echo of the rigor of the Vorkurs Stakes: Albers's legacy persists even in the former student's administrative errands

Twombly, in blue jeans, a sketchbook in hand, stands in profile next to the colossal fragment of the hand of the emperor Constantine, absorbed in contemplation; Rauschenberg frames it tightly Atmosphere: Being crushed by vanished grandeur, like Fuseli's despair before the same fragments Stakes: The young American facing the weight of European antiquity

Around the couple in crisis and baby Christopher, Rauschenberg hangs his modular white canvases as a backdrop and projects his slides, while Cage reads, Cunningham dances, Tudor plays, and Olson recites: the first American theatrical synthesis of the arts. Atmosphere: summer heat, the college's hospitality, joyful eclecticism Stakes: the rejection of Albers and the birth of an art of openness; a prototype of the Happenings

Olson reads poems from the top of a ladder; behind him, Rauschenberg's white paintings; Édith Piaf crackles at high speed; Cunningham dances with a stray dog that wandered onto the chaotic stage. Atmosphere: Slapstick chaos, ritual mocked Stakes: The exact negation of GLYPH: chance and Zen replace myth and rite

In an arrangement of chairs in four triangles and White Paintings in a cross, the performers occupy overlapping time slots: poetry readings, dance, piano, records, a lecture on Zen, upside-down slides, with nothing causally linked, but in strict timing. Atmosphere: A bath of light, images, movements, and noises (Artaud) Stakes: The birth of the happening

A calligraphed card arrives: a black wash cut into bold graphic panels, sketches of pots, lists of discussions, demonstrations, and faculty; on the program, two weeks on form, mass production, master and apprentice, the relation between craft and art. Atmosphere: A Japanese-inspired aesthetic, ink and paper, the promise of an East-West encounter. Stakes: Bringing together the Bauhaus, England, and Japan in a single room in rural America.

On arriving, Leach announces that since he does not know the materials at hand, he will not demonstrate and will only lecture; under pressure from the audience, he gives in. Hamada, by contrast, declares he can make do: he gathers clays and glazes on the hillside in front of the workshop, ties weed stalks in a bundle to make brushes, and works at the wheel before potters and students, using the thrown piece not as an end but as a starting point for other manipulations. Words: Hamada: he could “make do” with the materials on hand. Atmosphere: Emulation between two masters, an audience of potters and students taking the measure of American academicism. Stakes: Two conceptions of the craftsman facing the unknown: the caution of expertise against improvised adaptation.

A gin bottle filled with water, two glasses, feigned and real drunkenness mixed; sun, dust motes; a view through the open door across the hall to the light on the mountain; an exchange of blue jeans; the dinner gong from across the lake; a slow walk, apart, a splitting head Atmosphere: Luminous, suspended, melancholy Stakes: The idyll at its peak, already over

An obligatory civil greeting; Doyle asks about the barn, offers nails, bursts out laughing, slaps Dawson on the back; his eyes flash at the word “teach”; Dan frowns as they walk away Words: “How's that Tobacco Barn coming?” / “Slow.” / “You're damned RIGHT you will” / “That's OAK!” / “That oak is gonna teach you.” / Dan: “He sure has it bad.” Atmosphere: Repeated Southern laughter, surface warmth, an underlying threat Stakes: A working friendship broken by college politics

Face to face on the board, each on his nail; Dawson notices the strange color (lead and violet) of his nail and realizes it is dark Words: “The Goddamned thing's changed color!” / “Hey! Let's quit! For Christ's sake — it's NIGHT!” / “Well by God, so it is.” / “Beautiful.” / “It is.” Atmosphere: Sudden darkness, the daze of work, peaceful companionship Stakes: Total absorption in the gesture, to the point of losing track of time

A quarrel over where the saw was yesterday; Dan turns red, runs off, brandishes the saw Words: “Here — HERE is your saw!” Atmosphere: Exasperation, resentment, shame Stakes: The nervous tension of exhaustion

Working on Boulez's Second Sonata, the pianist Tudor admits to his companion Richards that the score is not his real problem. Words: He confides that the sonata is complicated, but that his problems are not with the notes but with the music. Atmosphere: The couple's intimacy at work, an intellectual confidence. Stakes: This confidence leads Richards to Artaud and from there to the matrix of The Theater and Its Double in English.
Exhibition “New Work by Josef Albers — Homage to the Square et Transformation of a Scheme” Gallery press release, January 7-26, 1952

Huss approaches Forbes again, who refuses: he no longer feels close to Black Mountain either in spirit or in knowledge of the place. He estimates that he has given more than $20,000 in all and has done his part. More than $20,000 given in all; letters of January 20 and March 12, 1952 Consequences: The loss of a major donor

Elaine and Mercedes Matter, the only women on the Club's voting committee; on January 25, the panel “Abstract Expressionism II” with Gottlieb, Holtzman, Diller, and Busa; in April, the only woman on “Integration of Art and Architecture” (with Denby, Hendler, Kiesler) and “Problems of the Engaged Artist” (with Newman, Navaretta, Abel, Hendler); on May 14, she organizes the panel “New Poets,” introduced by O'Hara, with Ashbery, Guest, Schuyler, and Rivers as moderator

Invited to give a weeklong course to architecture students and teachers, Albers is received as a celebrity: put up at the best hotel, feted by architects, academics, and the American cultural attaché; he writes four letters to Anni during the week; all his talks are recorded; he speaks more Spanish than in Mexico. The city has grown enormously since his first visit (1934-12, i.e., December 1934); the questions never stop Consequences: Illustrates his undiminished love of teaching after thirty years
Photograph of Albers teaching in Havana in February 1952, during his Yale period.

Laverne suggested introducing color; Asawa apparently did so by painting the pieces and probably by incorporating colored wire (Lanier–Laverne letters of February 4 and 12, 1952; letter from Laverne to Asawa of September 18, 1953).

Sixteen one-hour interviews on the history of Surrealism, broadcast February-June 1952 and published the same year as Entretiens 1913–1952; in them Breton defends the lyrical phenomenon in poetry and the example of Lautréamont. 16 one-hour interviews

At the faculty meeting where each student is reviewed, Fee is warmly praised by all; Dr. Dehn, formerly a professor at Heidelberg, stresses the contrast between the Fee of before and the citizen of today; Fiore confirms the growing sharpness Olson saw in December. Consequences: Olson's letter to Mrs. Dawson of February 28, 1952, reassuring her and Cara

“6 Students Talk with Mies”: an interview with Mies by students of the School of Design at North Carolina State College, published in LINE magazine, vol. 2, no. 1, February 1952, in the same state and at the same time as Black Mountain College. LINE magazine, vol. 2, no. 1 (February 1952)

Received as a celebrity, put up at the best hotel, feted by architects, academics, and the American cultural attaché; overflowing classes, teaching from morning to night, endless questions, everything recorded; he writes to Anni four times, feeling each day the freshness of his craft after thirty years Words: Everything he says is an absolute surprise; he uses more Spanish than in Mexico Atmosphere: Tropical excitement, the students' eagerness, the happiness of teaching Stakes: The old master rediscovers the pure joy of the classroom

Albers consults the archaeologist Junius Bird (conversation on March 11, 1952, letter of April 23, 1952), who points out that the length of the cloth is also limited by the amount of fabric that can be rolled onto the loom's lower bar. A Paracas Necropolis specimen 14 feet 7 inches wide by 47 feet 4 inches long. Consequences: Albers replies by proposing weaving from both ends toward the middle, with the last wefts inserted by needle.

De Kooning, ready to consider Woman I a failure, has taken the canvas off its stretcher when Schapiro visits him and encourages him to rework and finish the image. Consequences: The canvas is finished and shown at Sidney Janis in 1953.

De Kooning has judged Woman I a failure and taken it off its stretcher; Schapiro visits the studio and persuades him to rework the image and finish it. Atmosphere: A moment of discouragement turned into a decisive new start Stakes: The rescue of the work that will make the painter world-famous

Anni Albers dates and signs in New Haven her technical study proposing that the wide Peruvian fabrics were woven in several layers folded accordion-style on narrow backstrap looms. Dated “May, 1952”; conversation of March 11, 1952; visit from Isabel Guernsey on March 14, 1952; letter from Junius Bird of April 23, 1952. Consequences: The essay appears in On Designing (1961).

Tudor premieres Water Music at the New School before returning to Black Mountain; it is probably the work he plays during Theater Piece No. 1. A hybrid score: a steam whistle notated as a linear wave, an instruction in calligraphed capitals to transfer water from one receptacle to another

Alone with her diagrams, described samples, and reading notes, Albers unfolds the argument: thread counts, calculations of layers, Bird's objections, the answer of weaving from both ends toward the middle, the last wefts set by needle where they meet. Words: Quotations from O'Neale (“the wefts lie in straight lines such as can be explained only by a wide batten”) and Bird (“length is also limited by the amount of cloth which can be rolled and supported on the lower bar”), discussed point by point. Atmosphere: The concentration of a home workshop, graph paper, an exchange of scholarly correspondence. Stakes: Reviving in thought a technical gesture lost for two millennia.
A reply to his letter mentioning his poverty: it mentions work scholarships and invites him for a three-day visit. College brochure, 600 acres Consequences: The trip is organized

Four young people (two gay students from Rider College, Roger and Marge, a taciturn lesbian at the wheel of her new green Chevy, and Mary Ann Fretz, a student of Mary Reed's) set out in early June 1952; an almost nonstop drive, a night spent in the car near the sleeping town of Black Mountain (altitude 2,400 feet), hysterical laughter at imaginary ghosts. Green Chevy, windshield spattered with insects, Marge's left arm tanned and her right one white, a handwritten BLACK MOUNTAIN COLLEGE sign Consequences: Arrival at the college in the morning

Arrival around 9 a.m.: the place is deserted between two sessions; only a starved orange dog crosses the road; initial disappointment: the college looks like a run-down summer camp, a former resort acquired at the time of the 1940-41 move from the other side of the valley. 9 a.m., a flat millstone near the entrance, a worm-eaten bench under an apple tree, creosoted buildings, the sounds of insects and birds Consequences: First doubts about the choice

A woman in white, barefoot, in a knotted man's shirt and cream Mexican pants, a cigarette at her lips and an empty Mason jar in hand, crosses the road; it is Connie, who says “We've been expecting you,” invites the group for coffee on the screened porch of the dining hall, and admits there was a party the night before. An oversized man's shirt, a dark blond ponytail, a Mason jar, thick white cups Consequences: A warm first contact; Rumaker feels hope

The tour: the round dinner gong, Dinner Bell Circle, Hazel Frieda Larsen's wisteria-covered house, Lake Eden, the stone Quiet House built by a teacher and a student, and the glass science building, finished but unused because Natasha Goldowski considered it dangerous on its thin metal legs, sometimes used for language or writing classes. Kudzu imported from Japan against landslides, snakebite kits nailed to the rusty lampposts, Mount Mitchell snowcapped at nearly 7,000 feet Consequences: Rumaker feels his heart warm to the place

The physicist, head of the science programs, refuses to set foot in the finished structure perched on two thin posts and forbids her students to use it, convinced it is bound to tumble down the slope; she had taught briefly at Princeton after her postwar immigration. Two metal posts, a three-level all-glass structure Consequences: The building remains almost unused, except for language or writing classes

Rumaker spends the summer with Roger's family: packing the lupines and peonies cut at dawn by Roger's father into peach baskets shipped by train to the wholesale markets in Manhattan; then a job at the Automatic Voting Machine Company; dinners in the huge kitchen with a wood stove and coffee always simmering. An icy root cellar, old newspapers, peach baskets, the afternoon train to New York (more than 400 miles), an 1860s cherrywood ancestral bed

While Roger works at the ice cream drive-in, Rumaker hitchhikes to the cable ferry at Bemis Point and the Chautauqua concerts; he spots a young blond man in a navy blazer, always alone at the same ramp of the Amphitheater, and develops a hopeless crush, too fearful to approach. A cable ferry across Chautauqua Lake, some twenty miles, Beethoven and Tchaikovsky from the orchestra pit

Rumaker works in the huge electroplating room across from a gruff old man, dipping dozens of metal straps into bubbling acid baths, thousands a day. The first week: two pairs of gloves, a pair of canvas pants, and new work shoes eaten away by the acid; a loop of acid-resistant wire Consequences: Good pay that lets him replace clothes and shoes, pay part of his board at the farm, and save for Black Mountain

Drive-in movies (The African Queen, free admission thanks to the land rented by Roger's mother), Genesee beer at the Mayville Inn, nighttime skinny-dipping in Chautauqua Lake with friends, two of them gay, outings to Chautauqua Gorge and Niagara Falls with Roger's parents. Genesee beer; nearly falling into the gorge and onto the rocks at the falls

In his report to President Griswold for 1951-52 (undated, probably June 1952), Albers judges the visiting critics program highly successful, proposes extending it to second- and third-year students to expose them to varied points of view, and asserts that these critics foster a freedom to learn as important as the freedom to teach. Typed report, JA Papers

Asawa and Cunningham design together the cover of Arts and Architecture with pasted photographs of Untitled (S.535). Asawa is credited there as “Ruth Lanier”: she has not yet taken back her maiden name despite Cunningham's advice. June 1952 issue; credit “Ruth Lanier”; pasted photomontage Consequences: Illustrates how long Asawa took to follow Cunningham's advice about her artist's name.

After nearly 600 miles nonstop, the four stop in the dark near the college's handwritten sign, windows up and doors locked, frighten themselves with imaginary ghosts, and laugh themselves into hysterics before dozing sitting up in the car. Atmosphere: Thick, wooded darkness, fatigue, nervous laughter, a few hours of fitful sleep Stakes: The threshold: the long-hoped-for arrival begins in fear and exhaustion

No one in sight; a starved orange dog slowly crosses the road and disappears behind the pines; Rumaker tries to explain away the emptiness (it is between sessions); the others seem to think it a wild-goose chase; they tacitly decide to wait, embarrassed. Words: “There's hope,” says Rumaker at the sight of the dog; perhaps it is because they are between sessions Atmosphere: The whir and drone of insects, birdcalls, dust, a drowsy place, disappointment Stakes: Doubt: is the college worth the 600 miles?

A barefoot woman in white, a giant cigarette, a jar in hand, crosses the road avoiding the stones; Marge orders Rumaker to catch her; he rushes over and apologizes for the number of visitors; Connie smiles her deep smile and invites them for coffee. Words: Marge: “Grab her… the last live one we catch all day”; Connie: “I'm Connie. We've been expecting you”; “We had a party last night” Atmosphere: Sun, dust, a warm smile contrasting with the desolation Stakes: The first human contact: the place opens up

While Connie drops off her milk jar, the group drinks coffee from thick white cups and discovers the lake, the white Studies Building, and snowcapped Mount Mitchell; Rumaker is still waiting to meet Connie's giant husband. Words: Connie tells them the lake is called Lake Eden Atmosphere: An opening view, lifting mists, a first easing Stakes: The landscape redeems the dilapidated buildings

Connie shows them Hazel Larsen's house, the Quiet House, the unused science building, and tells of Natasha Goldowski's refusal; Rumaker silently worries about the rusty snakebite kits; Connie reassures him about the snakes, which mind their own business. Words: “There are rattlesnakes and copperheads… but they mind their own business” Atmosphere: Rising heat and humidity, thick kudzu, smiling unease Stakes: Rumaker moves from doubt to attachment: his heart warms to the place

Every evening, a few ramps away, Rumaker steals glances at the young blond man in a navy blazer with gold buttons, always alone in the same spot; too terrified to approach. Atmosphere: Beethoven and Tchaikovsky in the night, a feverish, hopeless crush, the safety of fantasy Stakes: Desire under terror, sexual loneliness before BMC

In July, the Tworkov family (with the two daughters, Hermine and Helen) brings new vitality; in August comes Franz Kline, himself a crystal. M.C. Richards writes the words for a “French Farce Based on a Wagnerian Opera” in which almost the whole school takes part. The farewells at the end of August are sad, but the school is ready for the fall and a new contingent of women students. Play: A French Farce Based on a Wagnerian Opera, words by M.C. Richards Consequences: The secret end of a phase; the school redefines itself

A pork chop evening during the summer session. Helen asks Hermine to save her a portion; Connie secretly asks Charles to set aside a chop for Kate. Hermine, arriving slightly late, finds nothing to save, goes into the kitchen, discovers the covered plate on the shelf above the stove, and takes the chop: Kate's. Connie arrives with Kate on her hip and whispers to Charles; Olson stands up, grabs Kate in one motion, sets her on the palm of his right hand, arm outstretched (the child nearly eleven feet off the ground), and bellows like an Ahab or a Melville: WHO HAD STOLEN HIS DAUGHTER'S PORK CHOP? A deathly silence on the porch. A plate covered with another one upside down on the metal shelf above the stove; the baby ~11 feet off the ground, near the rafters; a screened porch looking out on the lake and mountains Consequences: Seven years later Hermine will ask Dawson to keep quiet; Olson apparently never knew
Jack Tworkov, his wife Wally, and their daughters Hermine (~11) and Helen (~9) come for a month in July 1952; Franz Kline is expected in August. Daughters aged about 11 and 9

An incident at dinner that the whole school saw; that evening Olson and Connie, alone in their apartment in South Lodge, share a suppressed hilarity: she knew the 1940 Dahlberg variation, and Dahlberg had thus taken his revenge, twelve years later, because of Black Mountain's unworkable honor system for food. Olson still angry, laughing as he curses “that son of a bitch”; a reference to the last line of Maximus Letter 16 Consequences: Olson will never speak of it: the incident brought to mind Connie, their daughter Kate, his departure with Betty and Charles Peter, then Betty's death

The day after a party at which Elaine de Kooning dipped hundreds of pennies in gold paint and scattered them on the lawn, and Nancy and Joan tied balloons to the trees, Elaine paints two grapefruits white with the seams and the Spaulding brand. The next day, Vicente (Elaine? the pitcher) on the mound, Franz at bat... Franz slips a grapefruit to the pitcher on the pretext of a conference on the mound. Everyone knows except Pavia; he swings and it splatters. After the cleanup: “All right, let's play.” Franz: “Just a second, I want to talk to Vincente.” Gilded pennies, balloons, painted grapefruits with the Spaulding brand

Years later, bases loaded, Dawson at bat, Franz pitching. He shouts to the outfielders to move back; they do not listen: he hits it over the left fielder's head, an inside-the-park triple. Next inning, the outfielders move back; Franz: “Aw hit the fuckin' ball.” Dawson holds out his hand chest-high over the middle of the plate; Franz puts the ball exactly there, and Dawson hits it over center field and scores, looking at Franz, who pretends to be fed up.

A pork chop dinner, general joy. Connie comes in with Kate on her hip and whispers in Charles's ear. Olson stands up, snatches Kate from Connie in one motion, sits her on his right palm, arm straight up (eleven feet off the ground), and bellows his Melvillean question. A deathly silence. Words: “WHO HAD STOLEN HIS DAUGHTER'S PORK CHOP?”; Hermine, in 1959, begging him not to tell anyone, since Olson would hear of it and be angry all over again Atmosphere: a summer evening, mountains in the distance, the smell of pork chops, then dizziness and silence Stakes: the honor of the community against a child's lie; a giant's anger

After dinner and the public incident, the couple alone; an exchange of looks, each keeping a straight face while laughing; she knows the 1940 version; Olson, still angry, laughs as he curses Dahlberg. Words: Olson breathes “that son of a bitch,” laughing Atmosphere: Hilarity mixed with anger, after the fact Stakes: Twelve years after Gloucester, Dahlberg is avenged; yet the incident will seal Olson's silence for life

Elaine and artist friends go skinny-dipping by moonlight; she writes to Ernestine Lassaw that her hair has not been so light nor her skin so brown in years. Letter to Ernestine Lassaw; the purchase of a refrigerator for her mother to replace the icebox, leaving her in her natural state: broke

Elaine finishes an article on Buckminster Fuller; after an evening of drinking with Burgoyne Diller when she was supposed to look at his paintings for an ARTnews article, she has nothing left but feathers in her head, which she used to dust off Bucky. ARTnews article on Diller postponed in a drinking bout

From 8:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m., Cage, perched on a stepladder, spoke about the relation of music to Zen Buddhism while a film was projected, dogs barked as they crossed the stage, and twelve people danced without rehearsal, with prepared piano, whistles, babies crying, and Édith Piaf records played at double speed on a turn-of-the-century machine. 8:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.; stepladder; 12 dancers; prepared piano; Édith Piaf records at double speed Consequences: Considered the first American Happening

After the closing concert (Beethoven's Ninth), Rumaker hitchhikes; a young man makes a sexual advance, is rebuffed, then in revenge speeds up to 90 and then 100 miles an hour on the country road. 100 miles an hour; tires screeching on the gravel of the farm driveway Consequences: Terror; immense relief at reaching the gravel of the farm

Around mid-August, in the cool early autumn of western New York (the leaves already reddening), a letter from Connie Olson: the work scholarship application is accepted, and he is expected in early September for the fall quarter. Mid-August, a sharp chill in the air Consequences: Joy: leaving behind the acid-eaten clothes and heading south

One evening in August 1952, Cage directs Theater Piece No. 1, widely considered the first Happening, bringing together nearly all the performing arts: dance, music, poetry. The author recalls that this event was only one among hundreds of performances at the college. It sprang up like a mushroom in the historiography Consequences: Becomes the emblematic event to which performance at BMC is reduced

One evening in August 1952, an untitled performance devised by Cage during the day and carried out that same evening: poetry readings (Olson, Richards), dance (Cunningham), prepared piano music (Tudor), Rauschenberg's paintings hanging from the ceiling, records played, films projected. No script, rehearsal, or costumes; each activity began and ended according to time brackets set by Cage. It would gain fame as the first Happening by the end of the decade. The projectionist's score: “Begin at 16 min. play freely until 23 min.”; the college calendar simply notes “a 'concert' by John Cage” on August 16, 1952, a possible date Consequences: Retroactively considered the first Happening; a lineage established by Michael Kirby in 1965, rather through Cage's classes at the New School (Kaprow, Brecht, Hansen, Higgins)

No photograph of the event exists; only one score by Cage survives. Francine du Plessix's diary: Cage on a ladder spoke about music and Zen Buddhism while a film was shown, dogs barked, Merce danced, a prepared piano played, whistles blew, babies cried, coffee was served by four boys in white, and Édith Piaf records spun at high speed on a turn-of-the-century machine. Weinrib: Cunningham chased by a dog, Rauschenberg playing popular records from the 1920s-30s, Olson handing out a poem written in parts and having the audience read it standing, Richards reciting Edna St. Vincent Millay from the top of a ladder. Litz: the whole evening in French, Richards arriving on horseback, or on some moving structure. Williams: projection of hand-painted 35 mm slides and of pasted colored gels. Cernovich: projection of fragments of a black-and-white silent film. The projection surface is disputed: a screen, the ceiling, or Rauschenberg's White Painting (Four Panel). Starting time noted as 8:30 p.m. in du Plessix's diary; Cage speaks until 4:30 (sic) according to the same diary Consequences: The event's mythical status owes much to the lack of documentation

The summer of 1952 is remembered for the premiere of Cage's Theater Piece No. 1 and for his recognition, helped by Rauschenberg's White Paintings, of silence as the key to 4'33''. In 1989 M.C. Richards drew from memory a plan of the room for William Fetterman, including what is believed to be Kline's Painting; most memories instead place the White Painting (Four Panel) hanging from the ceiling
Franz Kline is invited to teach painting in August 1952; Dawson says a very emotional goodbye to him at the station with Nancy.

Wolpe, a former Bauhaus student teaching at the college, protests against the chaos and walks out; others find it rather boring or an interesting experience, or admit that one was not meant to understand it literally. No photograph or film of the performance exists; the accounts contradict each other because the seating arrangement ruled out a single point of view Consequences: Contradictory accounts circulate

Cage, on a stepladder, talks for two hours about music and Zen while a film, barking dogs, twelve improvising dancers, prepared piano, whistles, screaming babies, and Édith Piaf at double speed are layered on top of one another. Atmosphere: jubilant, simultaneous chaos Stakes: The official birth of the American Happening

After Beethoven's Ninth, a young man picks him up hitchhiking and immediately gropes him; Rumaker refuses curtly; mad with rage, the driver floors the accelerator up to 100 miles an hour to frighten and punish him; he finally drops him off on the gravel of the farm. Atmosphere: Night terror, screeching tires, the black road to Jamestown Stakes: The price of refused desire in 1950s America

One evening in August 1952, Cage simultaneously directs dance, music, and poetry: the first Happening. Atmosphere: A summer evening, layered arts Stakes: The legendary event that eclipses hundreds of other performances

Chairs in a square facing inward, two diagonal aisles for the performers. Cage climbs a ladder and talks about the relation of music to Zen Buddhism with long silences; Olson hands out a poem in parts and has the audience read it standing; Richards recites Edna St. Vincent Millay from the top of a ladder; Cunningham dances, perhaps chased by a dog; Tudor plays a prepared piano; Rauschenberg shows paintings on the ceiling and plays popular records from the 1920s-30s; a silent film or painted slides are projected (screen, ceiling, or White Painting); four boys in white serve coffee; whistles, dogs, babies, Édith Piaf records at high speed. Words: Cage (1969): he had simply drawn on the resources of the community; Richards: let it roll over you, don't try to make sense of every thread Atmosphere: a hot August evening, a chaotic and yet serene three-ring show, no rehearsal, nothing predictable Stakes: the invention of the Happening: the spectator placed at the center, overwhelmed, with no single point of view

The spectators sit on chairs arranged in a square of four triangles converging without meeting, a cup at each place; Olson and Richards climb a ladder to read their poems; Rauschenberg shows his paintings, plays records, projects upside-down slides onto the canopy of White Paintings; Cunningham dances, harassed by a barking dog; Tudor probably plays Water Music on the piano; Cernovich no doubt projects films; Cage reads his lecture on Zen and Meister Eckhart; hot coffee is served during the performance; Wolpe protests and walks out; everyone has to swivel to follow simultaneous actions. Words: Wolpe grumbles against the chaos; some found it rather boring, others an interesting experience, still others felt one was not meant to understand it literally Atmosphere: sensory bombardment, intentional disorientation, a 360-degree panorama, the smell of coffee, barking Stakes: events with no causal link, each centered on itself: the audience called on to take part with the whole body

Twombly has won a travel grant from the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts in Richmond; Rauschenberg goes with him for several months in Europe and North Africa; Rauschenberg has already decided before leaving to give up painting for photography Travel grant from the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts; a portfolio of photographs of Twombly's paintings made by Rauschenberg Consequences: Photographs become his main medium of expression during the trip

Rumaker, having heard of the college at a lecture by Ben Shahn at the Philadelphia Museum in 1952, arrives in September 1952 with a work scholarship (like Ed Dorn). Consequences: Assigned first to the farm, then to the kitchen.

His first experience of segregated transportation: a white conductor shouting out the assignment of cars; overcrowded Jim Crow cars with no baggage rack or air-conditioning, Black passengers fanning themselves with funeral-home fans; at the bar, a Southern drunk expounds his doctrine; at Charlottesville, a fleeting jealousy of a clean-cut, classic UVA student; a dining car where Black passengers are confined to a single table. The cry: “White folks' coaches ahead! Colored folks' coaches behind!”; funeral-home advertising fans; respectable citizens at the bar; white tables, white tablecloths, silverware Consequences: Rumaker feels like a criminal and an outlaw, in imaginative solidarity with the Black passengers (in his head he belonged to the rear cars too)

After a night of dozing, breakfast in the dining car, then more than an hour of winding climb through the mountains toward the Swannanoa valley; the rising sun reddens the clay of the cuts; arrival around 7 a.m. at the gray station, then a taxi to the Gatehouse. A station of gray boards with separate waiting rooms; a second pot of coffee; a white heron in the reeds Consequences: Intense hope and excitement as they descend into the valley

No one in front of the dining hall, no one in the stone office; exhausted, Rumaker goes up to the Studies Building, finds a study door ajar with a single bare mattress, lies down on it, and sleeps for an hour. A bare mattress on the floor, the only furniture; wide, grimy windows; a smell of mildew and of oil paint and turpentine; a white heron fishing in the reeds Consequences: A feeling of having arrived where he might find the secret and direction of his life

Hazel Larsen, in a wheelchair (polio in childhood), secretary-treasurer and photography teacher, explains the terms: four hours a day, five days a week on the farm in exchange for tuition and board. She announces that Olson, on leave in Washington for “research,” may not teach until late fall. 4 hours a day, 5 days a week Consequences: Disappointment about Olson; a first room assignment with Jorge Fick

Jorge Fick, just arrived from Detroit, bursts in, asks what the hell he is doing there, learns of the imposed room-sharing, yells about that damned woman, goes to complain at the office, comes back furious, and orders Rumaker to move out. Boots clattering in the hall; a pale oval face, a black crew cut Consequences: Rumaker installed in the men's dormitory upstairs, his bed near the door

Rumaker discovers the dormitory of about eight beds under the steep slopes of the roof; he meets Eric Weinberger (bearded, long black hair, very gentle, a New Yorker, several years at the college), Terence Burns (slight, glasses, auburn hair, a writer-painter from Providence, impeccable French, also a work scholar on the farm), and a Korea veteran in khakis pressed to the millimeter (GI Bill). Eight beds; unpainted pine walls gone dark; a shared shower and toilets with no privacy; a dime would bounce off the veteran's folded blanket; a mattress on a box spring, a small dresser Consequences: Rumaker counts himself happy after the misadventure with Jorge

Two former students live as recluses in the room next to Jorge's: Grady, red-haired, a pipe smoker, a glutton for books piled from floor to ceiling on a dirty bed, in debt to the librarian Nell Rice; Harmon, slim, mustached, talkative, and gentle. Sleeping by day and foraging in the kitchen at night, they have the palest skin on campus, and no one knows what they are studying. A characteristic heavy smell despite the bathroom in between; rare baths Consequences: Liked by all, and so tolerated

Before classes, an initiation to the farm: cutting the withered stalks of the harvested corn with a knife and tying them in bundles to be chopped into silage and blown into the silo, winter fodder for the cattle. Rumaker discovers an extensive and almost self-sufficient farm, with the house of the farmer Doyle Jones, lean, handsome, with very blue eyes, and his nervous but kindly wife. Knife, bundles, silo, cattle

Rumaker's first job as a work scholar: cutting with a knife the dried stalks in the already harvested cornfield and tying them in bundles with twine for the silage cutter and the silo (winter fodder for the animals). Don Jones, a painting student, shows the newcomers the ropes, notably Terence Burns and Rumaker. Terence recites Villon and sings “Auprès de ma blonde” as he works. Knife, twine, silage cutter, silo; Rumaker 6'2'' and under 125 pounds, a heavy smoker; a bright orange salamander with blue spots seen one afternoon Consequences: After a week Rumaker wonders whether he will last, but the work calms him and gives him an appetite
The hardest task: loading the very heavy milk cans onto a navy blue World War II surplus Jeep truck. Navy blue Jeep truck, WWII surplus, very heavy cans

At dusk, the line of workers comes back along the path through the woods, crosses the cold stream near Meadows Inn, and follows the dirt road along the lake to the kitchen, where Malrey and Cornelia have kept supper warm on the oil stove, often after sunset and after everyone else. A cold, fast stream; leaves of blinding brilliance on the Seven Sisters; supper on the porch; Cornelia's pot-boiled coffee; Don Jones's legs propped on a cane chair; snowcapped Mount Mitchell in the distance

Rumaker gets up early while almost everyone is asleep, eats eggs and grits and drinks Cornelia's strong black coffee alone on the porch, then smokes his first Home Run cigarette of the day, contemplating the mists on the lake and Mount Mitchell. Eggs, grits, a mug of black coffee, a Home Run cigarette, the first puff a “searing furnace blast,” morning mists on the lake Consequences: This moment calms his anxieties for a while

With Charles Olson on leave, Rumaker signs up for: Wes Huss's theater workshop (evenings, in the dining hall after supper); Hilda Morley's metaphysical poetry (afternoons, in the library); Natasha Goldowski's modern physics (mornings, in the hall of the Meadows Inn apartment she shares with her husband and former student Eric Renner); French tutoring with Madame Goldowski (mornings, in the back parlor of Streamside). 35 students enrolled in all in the fall of 1952

Rumaker chops bundles of corn on a conveyor while the silage is blown into the silo, where Fee Dawson and Ben jump to pack it down. Doyle speeds up the conveyor before nightfall; Rumaker drops his pocketknife into the metal innards, jamming the machine. Doyle, furious, sends him to replace Fee in the silo; he works with Ben, packing the silage down by dancing on it, for hours until it is completely full at sunset, then climbs down dizzy. A pocketknife lost in the conveyor, metal rungs in the silo's slot, boards slid into the slot as it fills, a silo several stories high, the summery smell of chopped cornstalks Consequences: The next morning, Rumaker asks Hazel Larsen for a job in the kitchen

One Sunday morning in early September, Rumaker walks several miles beyond the farms; he sees only livestock and vicious barking dogs, suspects that all the farmers are at church (the Bible Belt, the Sabbath), and feels eyes watching him from behind the curtains of every farmhouse. Barking dogs, cows and horses at pasture on every farm, even the poorest
Tommy comes back from a stay in England with a prewar MG, long, low, black, a two-seater with large spoked wheels. A black sports car, spoked wheels, “two-bucket seater”

After one of Tommy's weeks-long disappearances, the MG comes back as a wreck on a flatbed truck, along with a bruised Tommy with a black eye: he had crashed at high speed at night into an apple truck on a back road in Tennessee. The car in a heap on a flatbed; Tommy bruised, with a black eye Consequences: Tommy no longer has his MG for his errands in Buncombe County.
